claims.text: Tungsten is a high-neutron-activation refractory element.
Specific combinations of Nb, Ta, Mo, and possibly Zr are low-activation alternatives to tungsten.
Replacing high-activation refractory elements with lower-activation elements in a refractory HEA will reduce production of long-lived radioisotopes.
The proposed elemental substitution can preserve the high-temperature mechanical performance required for fusion plasma-facing components.
The proposed elemental substitution can preserve irradiation resistance required for fusion plasma-facing components.
Conventional tungsten-containing refractory HEAs contain elements with relatively high neutron activation.
Traditional tungsten plasma-facing materials can suffer from brittleness.
RAFM steels have insufficient high-temperature performance for the proposed plasma-facing application.
Replacing tungsten with a combination of Nb, Ta, Mo, and possibly Zr can form a new low-activation refractory HEA.
Elemental substitution alters the phase stability of the HEA.
Elemental substitution alters the microstructure of the HEA.
Changes in phase stability and microstructure will preserve or enhance high-temperature mechanical strength.
Tailoring elemental makeup to favor low-neutron-activation elements modifies the alloy's response to neutron irradiation.
Careful phase and microstructural design can maintain the intrinsic high-temperature and irradiation resistance of refractory alloys.
The optimized HEA will exhibit significantly lower residual radioactivity after irradiation than conventional tungsten and RAFM materials.
The optimized HEA will maintain tensile strength and ductility at temperatures up to approximately 1000 degrees Celsius.
The optimized HEA will outperform conventional tungsten-based materials in plasma-facing applications.
